title: Profiling Mixed CPU/GPU Pipelines
blurb: Tests why whole-process timing hides the real effect of a fix, isolating the loop, measuring GPU busy time with nsys, labelling phases with NVTX ranges, computing GPU utilisation, and the order of fixes for an idle GPU.

questions.prompt: Why did whole-process timing show only a 1.12x speedup for a fix worth 2.45x?
options: The GPU slowed down in the second run to match the CPU.
About 1.1 s of shared startup cost swamped the loop.
Whole-process timing counts the GPU twice, once per transfer.
The vectorised version had a bug that undid half of the gain.
questions.explanation: import torch took about 780 ms and CUDA init about 185 ms in both versions. Fixed costs dilute a real per-iteration difference.

questions.prompt: The slow loop took 239.9 ms and the fast loop 97.9 ms for 20 batches. What is the speedup? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 239.9 / 97.9 = 2.45, more than double what whole-process timing suggested.

options: Comparing whole script runs with shell time
Timing the import of torch separately from the loop
Instrumenting the script with perf_counter calls
Timing CUDA initialisation as its own region
questions.explanation: Whole-process numbers include startup costs common to both. The fix is to time the region of interest inside the script, as the other three options do.

questions.prompt: Which nsys reports give total GPU-side work for kernels and memory copies?
options: nvtx_sum and osrt_sum
The timeline view only, with no text reports
cuda_gpu_kern_sum and cuda_gpu_mem_time_sum
cuda_api_sum alone
questions.explanation: Summing kernel time and memory-copy time gives GPU busy time directly from real records. nvtx_sum reports labelled ranges.

refLinks.label: §56.2.3 nsys Measures GPU Busy Time Directly, Not by Inference

questions.prompt: GPU-side work was 0.851 ms in the slow pipeline and 0.849 ms in the fast one. What does that confirm?
options: The GPU got faster in the fast pipeline, which explains the speedup.
The GPU did no work at all in either version.
The fix was entirely on the CPU side. The GPU did the same work.
nsys failed to record the fast pipeline's kernels.
questions.explanation: Only the preprocessing code changed, so the GPU's work stayed the same. The 2.45x came from the CPU side.

options: Profiling a representative number of loop iterations
Profiling a single iteration or a very short run
Writing the profile to a named output file
Summarising the profile with nsys stats
questions.explanation: nsys needs enough activity for a meaningful picture. One iteration can also be dominated by first-launch effects.

questions.prompt: What do NVTX ranges add over nsys's whole-run totals?
options: Hardware counters such as warp stalls for each kernel launch
A second GPU to run the labelled code on in parallel
Automatic fixes for the slowest phase they find
Time per named phase, such as preprocess, from one run
questions.explanation: range_push and range_pop tag everything inside with a label, and nvtx_sum reports time per label. No two-run comparison is needed.

refLinks.label: §56.2.4 NVTX Ranges: Labelling Which Phase the Time Belongs To

questions.prompt: A script has NVTX ranges but nvtx_sum comes back empty. What is the likely cause?
options: range_pop must be called before range_push.
nsys ran without --trace=cuda,nvtx.
NVTX only works on AMD GPUs, not NVIDIA ones.
The ranges were too short to be measured at all.
questions.explanation: Some invocations trace CUDA by default but not NVTX, and the report gives no hint that ranges were skipped.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter trust the median per range rather than the mean?
options: Medians are always larger, so they're more conservative.
nsys reports the mean in the wrong units.
A slow first iteration skews the mean badly.
The mean can't be computed for NVTX ranges.
questions.explanation: One slow first launch drags the mean and standard deviation. The median reflects steady-state cost.

questions.prompt: The fast pipeline had 0.849 ms of GPU work in a 97.9 ms loop. What is its GPU utilisation as a percentage? Give two decimal places.
Both utilisation numbers were under 1%. How does the chapter read that?
options: The method is broken, since utilisation can't be below 10%.
The GPU was faulty and should be replaced.
The task is tiny. The comparison is what counts.
The pipeline should move back to the CPU entirely.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls it an honest finding about a toy workload. Vectorising roughly doubled utilisation by shrinking the CPU wait. Bigger batches are the next lever.

refLinks.label: §56.2.5 GPU Utilisation: The Real Bottleneck, Quantified

options: Including memory-copy time in GPU busy time
Using isolated loop time as the denominator
Computing utilisation from nsys records instead of guessing
Assuming it is GPU-bound without checking
questions.explanation: Low utilisation points at the CPU side or batch size. Tuning kernels that barely run wastes effort.

questions.prompt: In what order does Procedure 56.4 suggest fixing low GPU utilisation?
options: Buy a faster GPU first, then measure again
Raise batch size first, then rewrite the GPU kernels
Preprocessing, then batch size, then streams
Overlap with streams first, then batch size, then preprocessing
questions.explanation: Cheaper fixes come first. Multi-stream overlap is the most complex and comes last.

questions.prompt: A training job's total duration on a managed service barely changed after a data-loader fix. What does the chapter suggest before concluding the fix failed?
options: Time each step inside the script, apart from startup and model loading.
Rerun the job on a larger instance to see if the fix shows up there.
Move the data loader to the GPU, since the CPU must be the limit.
Accept the result, since total job time is the true measure of any fix.
questions.explanation: Container startup and model loading are fixed costs, like import torch here. The SageMaker note says to compare the region you optimised, not total job wall time.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the two fixed, one-time costs that dominated the naive whole-process timing comparison in this chapter's Worked Example, and state their approximate measured durations.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `import torch` (~780ms) and CUDA context initialisation (~185ms), both present identically in both pipeline versions, together roughly 965ms of fixed, one-time cost swamping the ~140ms real difference between the two loops.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the GPU utilisation formula from Procedure 56.3 and state what its two inputs are measured from.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `utilisation_pct = gpu_busy_ns / (wall_clock_seconds * 1e9) * 100`. `gpu_busy_ns` is measured from `nsys stats` reports (`cuda_gpu_kern_sum` + `cuda_gpu_mem_time_sum`, summed across all real kernel launches and memory copies); `wall_clock_seconds` is the isolated loop's measured wall-clock time (from Procedure 56.2's instrumentation), not the whole-process time.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's two timing methods (naive whole-process: 1.12x; isolated-loop: 2.45x), explain specifically what the ~965ms of combined `import`+CUDA-init overhead did to the naive comparison's apparent speedup, arithmetically.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The ~965ms combined fixed overhead was added identically to both versions' total times: slow pipeline's real loop time (239.9ms) plus ~965ms fixed cost plus other overhead ≈ 1,599.1ms total; fast pipeline's real loop time (97.9ms) plus the same ~965ms plus overhead ≈ 1,432.8ms total. Because a large, equal constant is added to both numbers before they're compared, the *ratio* between the two totals (1,599.1/1,432.8 ≈ 1.12x) shrinks dramatically toward 1 compared to the ratio of the actual loop times alone (239.9/97.9 ≈ 2.45x). A fixed additive cost compresses any multiplicative difference between two numbers when it dominates both of them.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's measured GPU-busy times (0.851ms slow vs. 0.849ms fast, a difference of only 0.002ms) alongside the measured utilisation change (0.35% to 0.87%), explain why these two facts together prove the fix's benefit came entirely from the CPU side, not from any change in GPU work.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The GPU-busy times are essentially identical between versions (0.851ms vs. 0.849ms, a 0.002ms difference, well within measurement noise), direct proof the GPU performed almost exactly the same amount of real work regardless of which preprocessing code ran. Since the utilisation percentage is GPU-busy-time divided by loop wall-clock-time, and the numerator barely changed while the denominator dropped by more than half (239.9ms → 97.9ms), the utilisation increase (0.35% → 0.87%) is arithmetically forced to come entirely from the loop getting faster, not from the GPU doing more work, which is exactly the CPU-side-fix conclusion the chapter draws.

bookExercises.prompt: A team reports "we optimised our GPU training pipeline and cut total runtime by only 8%, so further GPU kernel optimisation probably isn't worth it." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what to check before accepting that conclusion.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before concluding GPU optimisation isn't worth it, check whether that 8% figure was measured as whole-process wall-clock time or as an isolated per-iteration/per-epoch measurement. This chapter's own example showed a naive whole-process comparison reporting only a 1.12x speedup for a change that was actually a genuine 2.45x once import/init overhead was excluded. The real per-iteration effect of your GPU optimisation could be substantially larger than 8% once fixed startup costs are isolated out of the comparison."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 56.4 lists three fixes for low GPU utilisation in order (vectorize CPU code, increase batch size, overlap with streams) and warns against jumping straight to step 3. Using this chapter's measured results, explain what evidence would justify skipping to step 3 rather than trying step 1 or 2 first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Evidence that would justify skipping to step 3 (stream overlap) directly: utilisation is already reasonably high after trying steps 1 and 2 (vectorized preprocessing AND a batch size that's already been increased as far as memory or the problem allows), yet the CPU is still measurably idle-waiting for the GPU or vice versa within each iteration, i.e., steps 1 and 2 have been genuinely exhausted (not just assumed exhausted) and `nsys`'s timeline still shows serialized, non-overlapping CPU/GPU phases. Without that evidence, as in this chapter's Worked Example, where vectorization alone (step 1) more than doubled utilisation, jumping to step 3 would be solving a problem steps 1-2 might have already fixed for a fraction of the implementation complexity.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about CUDA streams and asynchronous memory transfers (`cudaMemcpyAsync`). Explain in your own words how overlapping CPU preprocessing of batch N+1 with GPU computation of batch N could improve on this chapter's Worked Example's fast pipeline (0.87% utilisation) without requiring any larger batch size.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Overlapping CPU preprocessing of batch N+1 with GPU computation of batch N (using `cudaMemcpyAsync` and a second CUDA stream) would let the CPU's preprocessing work happen concurrently with, rather than strictly before, the GPU's matmul on the previous batch. Instead of the pipeline's timeline being `[CPU preprocess batch N][GPU compute batch N][CPU preprocess batch N+1][GPU compute batch N+1]...` serialized end to end, it becomes closer to `[CPU preprocess N+1] running alongside [GPU compute N]`, hiding the CPU-side wait behind GPU compute time (or vice versa) that would otherwise sit idle. This could raise the fast pipeline's 0.87% GPU utilisation further without any change to batch size, since it addresses the *serialization* between CPU and GPU phases directly rather than changing how much work either phase does per batch.
